Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:27: Even according to the words of Rabbi Abba bar Chanina, who said he has no remedy, it is possible that his sin is great — in the manner of Doeg the Edomite, that although he was great in Torah, nevertheless the Holy One, blessed be He, called him wicked: "but to the wicked God says, what have you to do with declaring My statutes?" (Psalms 50:16); and they say in the chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 106b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Doeg: when you reach the passage of murderers and the passage of tellers of evil speech, what do you expound in them? "And you have taken My covenant upon your mouth" (Psalms 50:16) — Rabbi Ami said, Doeg's Torah study was only skin-deep.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:28: It might also be resolved, as Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, author of Menorat HaMa'or (letter 50), resolves it: what he said, that there is a remedy, refers to one who has not become habituated — he has a remedy so as not to continue the practice; but one who persists in the matter, with his hand still stretched out, is cut off through his sin. It is possible to expand his words based on what Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, explains in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, item 202), regarding the reason the teller of evil speech is worse than idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed (Arachin 15b) — he gives five reasons for this, one of them being that the master of the tongue's repentance is difficult, because he may have spoken evil speech about many people and does not know who they are in order to appease them. Further, because of his great habituation, he cannot properly repent, since evil speech has become second nature to him. For this reason we can say he has no remedy. Concerning something similar it is also said in the Zohar (Parashat Metzora 53a) that he has no repentance; and this is difficult, since it is written, "on the day of his cleansing he shall be brought to the priest" (Leviticus 14:2) [implying repentance is possible] — rather, certainly it speaks of one for whom evil speech has become a natural habit, and he cannot purify himself from it; and the intent of "he has no repentance" is that his repentance is difficult, until he properly repents.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:29: In Eleh HaDevarim Rabbah (Parashat Shoftim 9) it says that in the days of Saul they did not merit the building of the Temple because there were tellers of evil speech among them — Doeg and the Ziphites. But in the days of Ahab, even though they were idol worshipers, because there was no evil speech among them, they were victorious in war. Further there, another interpretation: Rabbi Muna said, whoever speaks evil speech removes the Shechinah from below to above; know this from what David says, "my soul is among lions, I lie among those who are set on fire, the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword" (Psalms 57:5); what is written after it? "Be exalted above the heavens, O God..." (Psalms 57:6). David said, Master of the universe, what should the Shechinah do below? Remove the Shechinah to the firmament — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:30: See how harsh is evil speech — worse than bloodshed, forbidden relations, and idolatry: worse than bloodshed, since it is written, "my iniquity is greater than can be borne" (Genesis 4:13); worse than forbidden relations, since it is written, "how then can I do this great wickedness" (Genesis 39:9); worse than idolatry, since it is written, "alas, this people has sinned a great sin" (Exodus 32:31). But regarding tellers of evil speech, it is written not "great" (masculine) nor "great" (feminine) but "great things" (plural), as it is said, "may the Lord cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks great things" (Psalms 12:4); therefore it is said, "death and life are in the hand of the tongue" (Proverbs 18:21).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:31: Another interpretation: "death and life are in the hand of the tongue" — do not say, "since permission has been given to me to speak, I will say whatever I wish" — the Torah has already warned you, as it is said, "guard your tongue from evil" (Psalms 34:14). And should you say you thereby lose out — no, rather you gain! And the holy spirit cries out, "whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles (mitzarot)" (Proverbs 21:23) — do not read "mitzarot" but "mitzara'at" (from tzara'at) — of his soul — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:32: Now, in what this passage says at its end, "from tzara'at of his soul," we find a fine resolution — for we see many people speak evil speech and have no plagues or tzara'at; rather, certainly the tzara'at and the plague are fixed in the soul: when the soul ascends above every night, all the holy ones separate from it and proclaim of it that it is impure, as it is said, "and unclean, unclean shall he cry" (Leviticus 13:45) — or after its departure from this world, if it did not perform proper repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:33: The words of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Parashat Ki Tazria 46b), lean somewhat toward this interpretation, even though he did not change the word "mitzarot" from its plain meaning; nevertheless, from the general matter, what is derived fits this reading. In these words, on the verse, "and man became a living soul (nefesh chayah)" (Genesis 2:7): he explains there that "nefesh chayah" is the neshamah, the supernal level among the levels of holiness in a person. And it further says: come and see, whenever this holy neshamah attaches itself to a person, he is beloved of his Master; how many guardians guard him from every side; he is marked for good above and below, and the holy Shechinah rests upon him. But when he strays from his way, the Shechinah withdraws from him, and the holy neshamah does not attach itself to him; and from the side of the strong evil serpent, this spirit is aroused, roaming and going in the world — for it rests only in a place from which the supernal holiness has withdrawn — and then the person becomes defiled and blemished in his flesh, in the appearance of his face, in everything.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:34: Come and see, because this "nefesh chayah" is supernally holy, when the holy earth [Malchut] draws it within her and it becomes comprised within her, then we call it "neshamah" — and this is what ascends above and speaks before the holy King, and enters through all the gates, with none to prevent it; therefore it is called "the speaking spirit," for all other souls have no permission to speak before the King except this one. Therefore the Torah proclaims and says, "guard your tongue from evil..." and it is written, "whoever guards his mouth and his tongue" — because if his lips and tongue speak evil words, those words ascend above, and when they ascend, all proclaim and say, "Remove yourselves from around the evil word of so-and-so; clear the place for the way of the mighty serpent" — then the holy neshamah is removed from him and withdraws, and cannot speak, as it is said, "I was dumb with silence, I held my peace" (Psalms 39:3), and that neshamah ascends in shame, in the distress of everything, and they do not give it a place as before. Therefore it is written, "whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul (nafsho) from troubles" — "nafsho" certainly, that soul which used to speak becomes silenced because of the evil speech, and then the serpent is summoned, for everything returns to its place. And when that evil word ascends through known paths and rests before the mighty serpent, how many spirits are aroused in the world, and a spirit descends from that side and finds that this person has aroused himself with an evil word, and that the holy speaking spirit has been removed from him — then it rests upon him and defiles him, and then he is a leper.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:35: Just as a person's punishment comes about because of an evil word, so his punishment comes when a good word comes into his hand and he could speak it [but does not], for he thereby blemishes that speaking spirit, since it was arranged to speak above and speak below, all in holiness — all the more so if the people go in a crooked path and he could speak to them [in rebuke] and remains silent and does not speak, in the manner I have said, "I was dumb with silence, I held my peace from good; and my sorrow was stirred" (Psalms 39:3), with the strokes of impurity. This is what King David the king means by "in this I was stricken and turned away from" [i.e., punished] — as it is written, "turn to me and be gracious to me" (Psalms 86:16), as it is said, "and Aaron turned" (Numbers 12:10) — so far his words. From this passage we learn how great the punishment for evil speech is.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:36: At the beginning of the passage "this shall be the law of the metzora," in these words: Rabbi Chiya said, whoever utters evil speech, all his limbs become defiled and he deserves to be shut up [quarantined], because that evil word ascends and arouses an impure spirit and becomes defiled; it comes to be defiled, they defile him; through the word below, another word is aroused.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:37: Further, there Rabbi Yehudah said: "this shall be the law" — certainly, corresponding to it, in order to exact retribution from that one who "spreads a bad name," "on the day of his cleansing he shall be brought to the priest" — what does this teach us? It implies that whoever has an evil tongue, his prayer does not enter before the Holy One, blessed be He, for an impure spirit is aroused against him. Once he returns in repentance and accepts repentance upon himself, what is written? "On the day of his cleansing he shall be brought to the priest" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:38: And it says, "once he returns in repentance, and accepts repentance," for two kinds of repentance are needed: first, immediate repentance, which is self-abasement, as explained, of blessed memory, "a healing tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it is a wound to the spirit" — and therefore the Torah commanded [the use of] hyssop, which indicates lowliness and self-abasement. And further, "accepts repentance upon himself" — meaning, to accept upon himself not to return to that sin again, as it is said, "and let them not turn again to folly" (Psalms 85:9).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:39: Included in the repentance needed for evil speech is that he make himself mute regarding worldly words, as though he had no tongue — for concerning the master of the tongue it is said, "may the Lord cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks great things" (Psalms 12:4), and the intent of "cut off" is that his tongue is cut off in Gehinnom the same number of times he spoke evil speech, in the manner done for other transgressions — every limb with which he sinned is judged until all that evil he did is digested [purged]. Therefore he must cut off his tongue from speaking while still alive, and suffer in place of what he enjoyed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:40: Now, having discussed the punishment for evil speech, let us discuss the divisions of evil speech; and although we have not written everything found in the words of our Rabbis, so as not to be lengthy, this reminder suffices for the intelligent reader to arouse his heart to repent. I have seen fit to abridge the words of Rabbeinu Yonah in the Gate of Repentance and other authors who speak on this matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:41: The first division of evil speech, concerning which we were commanded in the Torah not to speak it and not to accept it, as it is said, "you shall not accept a false report" (Exodus 23:1) — its essence is speaking disparagingly of one's fellow, even if he speaks the truth; for if he speaks falsehood, he is found to "spread a bad name." One who speaks disparagingly of his fellow intends to make his reputation stink and to demean him, and therefore reveals the abominations of his ancestors, even if not in his presence — and this is the class of true tellers of complete evil speech. If he was a penitent and someone tells of his earlier sins, whether in his presence or not, this carries a great punishment, for the sins of one who has repented become as merits, and this shames him, which is improper. Further, others who hear this shaming of the penitent will refrain from repenting themselves, and thus he locks the door of repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:42: Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory, wrote that in one respect, the sin of one who tells evil speech about a true matter is greater than one who speaks falsehood — because people will believe him when he tells honest matters about his fellow, and his stench will rise before them, and he will be despised in their eyes; even one who has regretted his sin and repented, his blemish will remain in people's mouths. And if a person sees his fellow transgress a Torah matter in secret, he should not reveal his sin publicly, for perhaps he has repented — particularly if he is a single witness, for one who testifies against his fellow alone is given lashes for rebellion. It is not fitting to reveal these except to a discreet sage who will not tell the masses; and if he knows they will believe him as though he were two witnesses, then he should tell it so that that sage may come to hate him [the sinner] — so they say in the chapter Arvei Pesachim (113b). But it is permitted to distance oneself from his company and hate him until one knows he has turned from his evil way.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:43: Regarding matters between one person and another, such as robbery, oppression, and fraud, one may tell these matters to people, for they said, of blessed memory (Ketubot 87b), that a single witness can obligate an oath. And if the sinner is a Torah scholar and a fearer of sin, it is fitting to think that he has truly repented, as they explain, of blessed memory (Berachot 19a): if you see a Torah scholar commit a transgression by day, do not entertain suspicion of him at night, for he has certainly repented. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Tikkunei Zohar 141b) that concerning this it is said, "his body shall not remain all night upon the tree" (Deuteronomy 21:23) — regarding the corpse of the sin he committed upon the Tree of Life — for he has certainly repented. Concerning this we find that Joseph the Righteous was punished for bringing evil reports of his brothers to his father, as they say in Bereshit Rabbah (84:7), on the verse, "and Joseph brought" (Genesis 37:2), as Rashi explains — and he was punished for all three [reports].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:44: But a person whom we know to be entirely wicked, with no fear of God before his eyes, it is permitted to publicize him and speak of his disparagement, to make transgressors odious in people's eyes, so that the souls of the listeners be repulsed by the evil deeds — for it is said, "the fear of the Lord is to hate evil" (Proverbs 8:13), and they say, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 52a), a wicked man, son of a righteous man, is permitted to be called "wicked son of a wicked man"; a righteous man, son of a wicked man, is permitted to be called "righteous son of a righteous man."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:45: Now, if you see a person speak a matter or do a deed that could be judged either favorably or as meritorious, if he is one who fears Heaven, you are obligated to judge him favorably, even if the matter leans more toward the side of guilt. And if he is among the intermediate people who are careful about sin but sometimes stumble in it, you should incline the doubt to judge him favorably, as they said (Shabbat 127b), "whoever judges his fellow favorably, the Holy One, blessed be He, judges him favorably" — and this is a positive commandment of the Torah, "in righteousness shall you judge your fellow" (Leviticus 19:15). And if the matter leans toward guilt, you should treat it as doubtful and incline it toward guilt. And if that person's deeds are mostly evil, or you have found that there is no fear of God in his heart, you should incline his deeds and words toward guilt.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:46: Included in this class, that of one who speaks true evil speech, is one who, even between himself and his own mind, recalls the evil deeds of his fellow's ancestors — this transgresses what is written in the Torah, "and you shall not wrong one another" (Leviticus 25:17), which speaks of wronging with words. If he tells the deeds of his ancestors before others, our Rabbis say concerning this (Bava Metzia 58b) that whoever whitens (shames) his fellow's face in public is like one who sheds blood, descending to Gehinnom and never ascending. Therefore a person must be careful to distance himself from speaking of people's blemishes and their disparagement, for a person's speech testifies concerning himself and the hidden matters within him — for a proper person speaks in praise of people and does not wish to tell of their disparagement, but the unfit person's whole desire is to speak of people's blemishes, because, being himself unfit, he wishes to disqualify others, as we learn in Kiddushin (70a): it was taught, whoever disqualifies [others], disqualifies with his own blemish [i.e., he sees his own faults in others] and does not speak in praise of the world; Shmuel said, he disqualifies with his own blemish. And if the blemish is well known regarding him and his family, he must be even more careful to guard his tongue from mentioning it in any manner, even by hint, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say in the chapter HaZahav (Bava Metzia 59b), regarding "for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:20).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:47: Also included in evil speech is one who tells it in a jesting and light manner, meaning that he speaks not out of hatred, and this is what King Solomon, peace be upon him, said: "as a madman who casts firebrands, arrows, and death, so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, Am I not joking?" (Proverbs 26:18-19). Likewise one who speaks by way of hints, telling the story in an innocent manner as though he does not know it is evil speech, but when protested against, says, "I did not know that these were so-and-so's own deeds." Also one must be careful not to tell evil speech about charity collectors who are fit, for whoever tells evil speech about them, saying they steal and show favoritism to whomever they wish — there is no measuring the punishment for this evil speech, for he shames servants of the Lord and their children and relatives, and prevents good people from doing commandments, and perhaps causes future collectors not to act properly [out of fear of such accusations].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:48: The second division is going about as a talebearer (rechilut), and we were warned about this in the Torah, "you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people" (Leviticus 19:16), and this is included in the class of tellers of evil speech, as they say, of blessed memory (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:2), regarding Doeg the Edomite, that he was a master of evil speech and a talebearer, spreading words — for "rachil" refers to one who carries words from this one to that one: "so-and-so said such-and-such about you, he did such-and-such," like this peddler (rocheil) who goes around the towns.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:49: Included in talebearing, one must be careful of what they say, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 29a): it was taught, from where do we learn that a judge should not say, "I acquit, but my colleagues convict — what can I do, since they are the majority"? Therefore it is said, "you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:50: Talebearing increases hatred, and it follows that it demolishes the pillar of the world, which is peace (Avot 1:17). And they say, of blessed memory (Niddah 61a), regarding talebearing, that although it is forbidden to accept it and hate one's fellow because of it, nevertheless one should not treat the matter as unimportant, but should guard his soul and be wary of the matters — the proof being from Gedaliah ben Achikam, who because he did not take heed to accept the evil speech at all, was killed, as explained there, of blessed memory. And they say, of blessed memory (Devarim Rabbah 5:9), that in the generation of Saul there were troublemakers like Doeg and the Ziphites, and although they [Israel] were righteous, they would go down to war and fall; but in the generation of Ahab, where there were no informers, they would go down to war and be victorious, for Obadiah hid a hundred prophets and no one revealed it, even though Ahab and his generation worshiped idols.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:51: One who stirs up strife between brothers and friends and brings hatred between them is worse than all the divisions of evil speech, in the manner it is said, "and one who sows discord between brothers" (Proverbs 6:19), and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say (Vayikra Rabbah 16:1) that the seventh [thing listed there] is worse than all of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:52: Also included in talebearing is not revealing his fellow's secret, and this is forbidden — for they say in Yoma, first chapter (4b): from where do we learn that one who tells his fellow a matter is [under the obligation] "do not reveal," that it is forbidden to reveal it? As it is said, "and the Lord spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, saying" (Leviticus 1:1) [implying privacy of communication]. Whoever reveals a secret departs from the way of modesty; it seems to me that regarding this it is said, "a talebearer reveals secrets" (Proverbs 11:13) — meaning, one who is called a talebearer is one who reveals secrets, and he has the punishment of an actual talebearer, who is one of the five classes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:53: The third division is the "dust" of evil speech, of which they say, of blessed memory, in Bava Batra (165a), that everyone stumbles in the dust of evil speech. This has four parts: the first, one who speaks excessively of his fellow's good qualities, for from praise of him comes his harm — so they say in the chapter Yesh (Arachin 16a). Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, explains (Gate 3, item 226) that this means he speaks of his good qualities in the presence of his enemy, and there is no one present at that gathering who could protest to the enemy and blunt his teeth. But if he praises a proper person who is well known for piety, even if an enemy is present, he may praise him, for everyone knows that he [the enemy] is an enemy and lies in his words. It seems to me that even though he speaks of his fellow's good qualities, he should not exaggerate excessively — such as things people won't believe — but should tell of matters and virtues that are plausible.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:54: Included in the dust of evil speech is one who says, "Where are there coals, if not in so-and-so's house, where meat is always roasting?" (Arachin 15b). Also included in this is one who lodges in his fellow's house and is treated well, and the next day goes out to the marketplace and says, "Blessed be so-and-so, for he slaughtered such-and-such an animal and prepared such-and-such," and the like; concerning this it is said, "he who blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him" (Proverbs 27:14) — for when this is heard, worthless people will gather at the host's house, and he will lose his money because of worthless guests (Arachin 16a). It seems to me that this is also included: if a person lends his poor fellow a dinar, the poor person should not praise him publicly, for perhaps the host's mind will not be equally disposed toward everyone, and he will come to a loss — perhaps they will not repay him properly — and one must be careful.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:55: Included in the dust of evil speech is what they say in the Gemara there (Arachin 15b), in these words: Rava said, anything said in the presence of the subject's master [i.e., openly] has no aspect of evil speech in it. Abaye said to him, all the more so this is brazenness and evil speech! He said to him, I hold as Rabbi Yosei, who said, "in all my days I never said anything and then took it back" — meaning, I never said anything about a person not in his presence and then suppressed it when he was present. But if he speaks of one who has sinned and did not first make known to the sinner's ear and rebuke him, it should be reckoned to him as evil speech, since it appears as though he flatters him [to his face] and reveals his blemish to others not in his presence — and further, they will say he does not speak the truth. But if he rebuked him and he did not listen, then he may make his sin known to people and they will not suspect him of wanting to cast blame on his fellow. Likewise, if the teller is established among the many as one who shows no favoritism, and whatever he says not in someone's presence he would say in his presence, and he is established as speaking only truth, then it is permitted for him to say those things.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:56: Further it says there: Rabbah bar Rav Huna said, anything said in the presence of three people has no aspect of evil speech in it — what is the reason? Your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend [so it will spread regardless]. However, if the matter said in the presence of three, or even many, was said as a secret, it is forbidden to reveal it, and so they say in Sanhedrin (31a): a certain student revealed a matter that was said in the study hall after twenty-two years, and Rabbi Meir expelled him from the study hall and said, "this one reveals secrets" — so far his words. Also included in the dust of evil speech, the Rambam writes (Hilchot De'ot 7:3), is that one should not say, "be quiet about so-and-so, I don't want to tell what I know about him" [implying something bad without stating it].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:57: The fourth division is the complainer (nirgan), concerning whom King Solomon, peace be upon him, said, "the words of a complainer are like wounds" (Proverbs 18:8). A complainer is a person whose way is to complain and grumble about his fellow, bringing forth complaints from his heart, saying, "So-and-so told me such-and-such, and his intent was only to insult me, and he meant me harm," even though he intended good for him, and he multiplies complaints and portrays himself as wronged, as though people rob him, insult him, and curse him for nothing; concerning this it is written, "a complainer separates close friends" (Proverbs 16:28), meaning he separates from himself a friend and companion. Whoever has this evil trait, just as he complains about people, so he casts words against Heaven, and thinks about the Name's kindness that its intent is to take revenge on His creatures and bring calamity to the world; and even when he sees a flow of good, he says that its outcome will be evil, as it is said, "and you murmured in your tents and said, Because the Lord hates us..." (Deuteronomy 1:27), and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said, do not increase complaint, lest you come to sin. The complainer, by his evil nature, is ungrateful, for he thinks the good done to him is evil, and repays evil for good. This evil trait comes from the evil of the heart, for from his heart's evil he views a person's good as evil, and brings his evil thought into action, speaking evil and complaining.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:58: The fifth division concerns vulgar speech, and Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him, wrote in the book Menorat HaMa'or (letter 56), in these words: we find that many people are compelled with whips, fire, and water, and by every kind of compulsion, to confess matters they have stumbled in, and they endure all the compulsions and do not confess any matter with their mouths that would obligate them, through their confession, to be executed — even though they see that it is only a temporary death, for they know clearly that today or tomorrow they will die anyway — nevertheless, in order to gain a temporary life, they endure their distress and accept all the sufferings in the world. All the more so should one be careful whom no one compels to say vulgar words, and who has no pleasure from this speech, but knows that in saying it, "his iniquity is greater than can be borne," and they will judge him with an eternal death — that he should seal and restrain his mouth from saying it! For whoever speaks vulgarly, his judgment is turned against him for evil, as we learn in the first chapter of Ketubot (8b): "therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men..." (Isaiah 9:16), and what is "and His hand is stretched out still"? Rav Chanan bar Abba said, everyone knows why a bride enters the wedding canopy [i.e., for marital relations], but whoever speaks vulgarly and utters a vulgar word from his mouth — even if a decree of seventy years for good has been sealed for him, it is turned against him for evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:59: We also learn in the chapter Bameh Madlikin (Shabbat 33a): because of the sin of vulgar speech, many troubles and evils and harsh decrees are renewed in the world, and the young men of Israel's enemies die, and orphans and widows cry out and are not answered, as it is said, "therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men..." What is "and His hand is stretched out still"? Rav Chanan said, and so on. And Rav Chisda said, whoever speaks vulgarly, they deepen Gehinnom for him, as it is said, "a deep pit is the mouth of strange women" (Proverbs 22:14). Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] says, even one who listens and remains silent, as it is said, "he who is cursed by the Lord shall fall there" (ibid.).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:60: Therefore a person must purify his mouth from speaking vulgarity, for the holy mouth was created only to speak holiness, and one who speaks vulgarity abandons the path of modesty and decency, which are the finest qualities by which Israel is distinguished from the other nations, and shows about himself that he has no part in the holy nation — so far his words. I have abridged some of it so as not to be lengthy. Rabbeinu Yonah writes similarly in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, item 229).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:61: Regarding the punishment for one who soils his mouth, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Pekudei 249b), in the third chamber of the holy chambers, in these words: these are the four who stand and rebuke and excommunicate all those who utter from their mouth an unnecessary word and soil their mouths; these excommunicate him, and he remains [in this state] for forty days, during which his prayer is not heard and he does not enter within the curtain, remaining rebuked outside — so far his words. This shows he is rebuked and excommunicated, and for forty days his prayer does not ascend above. And it further says that whoever is excommunicated above, the guarding of his Maker withdraws from him, and his soul does not ascend above — and we shall quote the rest of its wording below.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:62: Further, in the chambers of impurity (there, 263b), in the first chamber, in these words: and from this evil spirit hang several other troops appointed to seize an evil word or a soiled word that a person utters from his mouth, and afterward utters holy words. Woe to them, woe to their lives — these are the people who cause these other troops to rule and to blemish a holy place; woe to them in this world and woe to them in the World to Come, because these impure spirits take that impure word, and when a person afterward utters a holy word, these impure spirits get there first and take that impure word and defile that holy word, and the person does not merit through it, and, as it were, the holy power weakens — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:63: Further, they say, of blessed memory (Avot D'Rabbi Natan, ch. 3): Rabbi Elazar said, a beautiful and praiseworthy person who utters a disgraceful word from his mouth — to what may he be compared? To a beautiful hall with a tanner's sewage pipe fixed in it — every passerby says, "How beautiful this hall is, except that there is a tanner's sewage pipe within it" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:64: The sixth division is that one should not utter a disgraceful word from his mouth; and although they said, "a person should always teach his students concisely," it is better to be somewhat longer in order not to utter a disgraceful word from his mouth, as we learn in the first chapter of Pesachim (3a): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, a person should never utter a disgraceful word from his mouth, for the verse twisted eight letters rather than utter a disgraceful word from its mouth, as it is said, "and of the beasts that are not pure" (Genesis 7:8) [rather than saying "impure" directly]. Rav Ashi said, nine letters, as it is said, "if there is among you any man that is not pure, by reason of an occurrence of the night" (Deuteronomy 23:11). Rav said, sixteen letters, as it is said, "and he said, It is an occurrence, he is not pure, surely he is not pure" (I Samuel 20:26) [rather than directly stating impurity]. And they elaborate further there, and it further says there: there were three priests; one said, "my portion came to me doubled" (referring to the showbread), one said, "my portion came to me like an olive," and one said, "like a lizard's tail." They investigated after him and found in him a trace of disqualification. This teaches that a person's speech testifies concerning him and his root.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:65: The pious author of Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Submission, ch. 6) writes, in these words: it is said of one of the pious ones that he passed by the carcass of a dog, very putrid, and his students said to him, "How putrid this carcass is!" He said to them, "How white are its teeth!" and they regretted having spoken of its disparagement. Since it is disgraceful to speak of a dead dog [disparagingly], all the more so of a living person; and since it is good to praise the carcass of a dog for the whiteness of its teeth, all the more so it is an obligation, according to this, to praise an intelligent person. His intent was to rebuke them so that they not train their tongues to speak evil, which would become their nature; and likewise, when they train their tongues to speak good, it will become their fixed nature, as it is written, "he does not slander with his tongue" (Psalms 15:3) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:66: The seventh division is not to give a bad nickname to one's fellow, for they say, of blessed memory, in Bava Metzia (58b): everyone descends to Gehinnom and ascends, except these, who descend and do not ascend — one who gives a bad nickname to his fellow, one who whitens (shames) his fellow's face in public, and one who has relations with a married woman. "Giving a nickname" and "whitening the face" are the same — [the Gemara clarifies:] it is necessary [to state both] even though he [the victim] is accustomed to being called by that name [publicly, so it seems less shameful, still it is forbidden] — so far his words. This equates giving a bad nickname with having relations with a married woman, which is one of the severe transgressions requiring death rather than transgression.
